Backups now contain your work, and you choose where they go.

## The defect this fixes

Settings had a button labelled "Export workspace". It produced a file, announced "your backup is ready", and that file held none of your data.

Measured on a real workspace holding 10 ideas, 31 drafts, 46 draft versions, 4 target audiences, 4 offers, 5 pillars, 10 voice rules and 64 tags: the export contained five directory names, two empty lists, and the file names of 70 execution logs. 573 rows in the database, zero in the export. It would have restored nothing.

## What a backup is now

**It holds your work.** A consistent snapshot of the database, plus your workspace files, in a single `.zip`. Everything you have typed: strategy, ideas, drafts and their versions, target audiences, tags, calendar.

**You choose where it goes.** A save dialog opens, with a dated default name so successive backups sort chronologically instead of overwriting each other. Closing the dialog cancels quietly, without announcing a file that was never written.

**You can restore it.** A new button in Settings, under Data. It reads the archive, asks you to confirm while naming what the archive contains ("10 ideas, 31 drafts, 4 target audiences"), copies your current database aside, and then replaces your workspace. No restart needed.

**It says what it did.** Saving and restoring both report the counts that were actually written, so the message can no longer contradict the file.

## What is deliberately left out

Execution logs are not included. They are raw transcripts of what was sent to the AI, they are reproducible, and Settings has a button whose whole purpose is to purge them. Putting them into a file you may store elsewhere or send to someone would work against that.

Previous backups are not included either, so archives never nest inside archives.

## Restoring replaces, it does not merge

A restore brings back the state of the moment the backup was taken. Tables the archive does not carry are emptied rather than left in place: a workspace half restored, with drafts from one state and their versions from another, is worse than a visible gap. Your current database is copied into the workspace `data` folder first, so a restore you regret is undoable.

An archive written by a newer version of GhostwrAIter is refused outright, naming the version needed, instead of being restored partly.
